title: CAN A PASTOR CURSE YOU FOR NOT GIVING AN OFFERING? THE TERRIFYING LIE THAT HAS KEPT TOO MANY CHRISTIANS AFRAID OF GOD
paragraphs: CAN A PASTOR CURSE YOU FOR NOT GIVING AN OFFERING? THE TERRIFYING LIE THAT HAS KEPT TOO MANY CHRISTIANS AFRAID OF GOD

When the pulpit becomes a place of financial threats, the offering plate becomes a weapon, and believers begin confusing a pastor's anger with God's judgment, one question must finally be answered: Does Jesus really punish people who cannot afford to give?
She had only enough money left to buy food for her children.
The bills were overdue. Her refrigerator was nearly empty. She had prayed all week for God to provide, and somehow, despite everything, she still found the strength to attend church that Sunday.
She wasn't there looking for a miracle wrapped in money.
She just needed to hear that God had not forgotten her.
But then the offering began.
The pastor stood behind the pulpit, his voice rising as he spoke about blessings, obedience, and financial sacrifice.
Then came the words that made her stomach tighten.
"If you refuse to give to God's work, don't complain when your finances collapse. You cannot expect God's protection while withholding what belongs to Him."
She looked down at the few bills folded inside her purse.
That money was supposed to feed her children.
And suddenly, she felt trapped between two fears.
If she gave it, what would her children eat?
If she kept it, would God punish her?
Her hands trembled.
Her eyes filled with tears.
And in that moment, something heartbreaking happened.
A woman who had come to church seeking the comfort of her heavenly Father began to fear that the same Father might harm her family because she could not afford an offering.
Now imagine Jesus standing beside that woman.
Would He threaten her?
Would He shame her?
Would He tell her that her children's hunger was the price of refusing to finance a ministry?
Or would He confront the religious system that had placed such a crushing burden on her shoulders?
Because before this article ends, we need to confront a question that reaches far beyond money.
When someone uses God's name to frighten you into giving, whose voice are you actually hearing?
The answer matters more than many Christians realize.
And it begins with something Scripture never teaches: that a pastor possesses personal authority to place a divine curse on a believer for refusing to give an offering.

A pastor may preach about generosity. He may teach biblical stewardship. He may encourage believers to support legitimate ministry needs. He may even warn against greed, dishonesty, and the spiritual dangers of loving money.
But he cannot manufacture a curse from God because you did not meet his financial expectations.
God's authority is not a weapon that belongs to the preacher.
And the Holy Spirit is not a debt collector.
Listen carefully to what the apostle Paul actually wrote.
In 2 Corinthians 9:7, the Greek text says:
ἕκαστος καθὼς προῄρηται τῇ καρδίᾳ, μὴ ἐκ λύπης ἢ ἐξ ἀνάγκης· ἱλαρὸν γὰρ δότην ἀγαπᾷ ὁ θεός.
A faithful translation is:
"Each one should give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver."
Two expressions deserve our attention.
The phrase ἐξ ἀνάγκης (ex anankēs) means "under compulsion" or "out of necessity or constraint."
And ἱλαρὸν δότην (hilaron dotēn) means "a cheerful giver."
Paul is not describing a congregation terrified into surrendering its last coins.
He is describing generosity that comes from a willing heart.
The surrounding context is a collection for believers in need. Paul encourages preparation, generosity, and integrity, but explicitly rejects coerced giving.
Think about that.
If a pastor tells you that God will destroy your finances unless you give him money, what has happened to the freedom Paul describes?
If you give because you are afraid of being cursed, are you giving cheerfully—or attempting to purchase safety?
And if the offering is obtained through spiritual intimidation, can the preacher simply call that pressure "faith"?
The Bible does not permit us to redefine coercion as worship.
But perhaps you have heard someone quote Malachi.
Perhaps the words still echo in your memory.
"You are cursed with a curse!"
That is Malachi 3:9, and it is one of the passages most frequently brought into discussions about tithing.
But what did God actually say, and to whom was He speaking?
In Malachi 3:9, the Hebrew text includes:
בַּמְּאֵרָה אַתֶּם נֵאָרִים
Bamme'erah attem ne'arim.
"You are cursed with a curse."
The Hebrew is serious. It refers to being under a curse, not merely experiencing disappointment or missing a financial opportunity.
But context changes everything.

Malachi was addressing the covenant unfaithfulness of Israel under the Mosaic covenant. The passage concerns tithes and contributions connected to Israel's worship, priestly provision, and covenant responsibilities.
In Malachi 3:10, God calls the people to bring the full tithe into the storehouse so there will be food in His house.
The text must be understood within Israel's covenant arrangement, including the agricultural and community responsibilities established in the Law.
It is not a blank check authorizing every modern pastor to threaten individual Christians with divine punishment whenever an offering falls short.
And it certainly does not establish that money placed into a particular preacher's hands determines whether God will protect your children.

The Old Testament law included tithes, offerings, provisions for Levites, and care for vulnerable people. Those arrangements cannot simply be transferred into the New Testament church without considering the work of Christ and the teaching of His apostles.
Christians differ over whether a ten-percent tithe remains a binding standard today or serves as a useful pattern for giving.
But regardless of that disagreement, no pastor receives biblical permission to extort offerings through personal threats.
Now consider the words of Paul in Galatians 3:13.
Χριστὸς ἡμᾶς ἐξηγόρασεν ἐκ τῆς κατάρας τοῦ νόμου
Christos hēmas exēgorasen ek tēs kataras tou nomou.
"Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law."
The Greek verb ἐξηγόρασεν (exēgorasen) carries the sense of redeeming or buying out.

Paul is speaking about Christ's redemptive work in relation to the law's curse. His message is not that Christians will never experience suffering, poverty, hardship, discipline, or consequences for sin.
It is that Jesus Christ has accomplished what human religious performance could never accomplish.
Our standing before God rests upon Christ's saving work, received through faith, not upon our ability to satisfy a minister's financial demands.
Read that again.
The blood of Jesus is not less powerful than an unpaid offering.
The cross did not secure redemption only for those who can afford a monthly contribution.
And no human being can reverse Christ's saving work by announcing a curse from a pulpit.
There is a difference between God's sovereign judgment, which Scripture takes seriously, and a preacher claiming the power to impose that judgment because someone did not give him money.
That distinction is essential.
Because the same Bible that encourages generosity also exposes religious leaders who exploit the vulnerable.
Jesus warned in Mark 12:40 about religious figures who "devour widows' houses" while maintaining an appearance of devotion.
And immediately afterward, Mark records the account of a poor widow who placed two small coins into the temple treasury.
Jesus saw her.
He noticed what everyone else could easily overlook.
He knew that she had given out of her poverty.
But look carefully at the setting.
The widow's offering appears in the context of Jesus' warning about religious exploitation and His coming judgment on the temple establishment.
Christ commends the significance of her sacrifice, yet the passage does not command church leaders to demand the last resources of impoverished people.
It certainly does not authorize anyone to threaten widows, struggling parents, or vulnerable believers until they surrender what they need to survive.
Jesus saw the widow's sacrifice.
He also condemned those who devoured widows' houses.
We must never use one part of His teaching to silence the other.
And there is another passage that deserves to be heard in churches where offerings have become a source of fear.
In 2 Corinthians 8:12, Paul writes:
According to what a person has. Not according to what he does not have.
Imagine how many tears might have been prevented if those words had been preached as faithfully as Malachi 3:10.
Paul continues in 2 Corinthians 8:13 that his intention is not for others to be relieved while the Corinthians are burdened.
His concern is fairness, generosity, and the mutual care of God's people.
That does not mean generosity never involves sacrifice.
Sometimes love gives at real personal cost.
But sacrifice offered freely is not the same thing as sacrifice extracted through intimidation.
A believer may choose to give generously in hardship.
A pastor must not exploit that hardship.
A believer may trust God while giving sacrificially.
A preacher must not promise guaranteed wealth in exchange for a donation.
But it must not pretend that God has delegated to its leaders the authority to sell His favor.
Perhaps this is where the story becomes painfully personal.
Maybe you have sat through a service where the pastor announced that anyone who did not give was blocking their own breakthrough.
Maybe you were told your business would fail.
That your children would suffer.
That sickness might enter your home.
That the enemy would gain access to your family because you had withheld an offering.
Maybe you gave money you did not have.
And afterward, instead of feeling joyful, you felt afraid.
You wondered whether the amount was enough.
Whether God was satisfied.
Whether the next unexpected expense was evidence that you had somehow failed Him.
And perhaps the most devastating part was that you stopped seeing God as a Father and began seeing Him as someone waiting for a payment.
If that happened to you, hear what Scripture says about the character of God.
Romans 8:1 declares:
"There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus."
That is not permission to become selfish.
It is not an excuse to ignore genuine responsibilities.
It is the announcement that condemnation is not the believer's relationship to God in Christ.
Romans 8:33 asks, "Who shall bring any charge against God's elect?"
And Romans 8:34 points to Christ, who died, was raised, and intercedes for His people.
Your ultimate security is not in a preacher's approval.
It is in Jesus Christ.
The New Testament also tells believers to test spiritual claims.
First John 4:1 says not to believe every spirit but to test the spirits to see whether they are from God.
A preacher's confidence does not prove his interpretation.
A microphone does not create divine authority.
A title does not make every warning biblical.
And an emotional atmosphere does not transform a financial demand into a command from heaven.
In Acts 17:11, the Bereans are commended for examining the Scriptures to see whether the things they were being taught were true.
They did not treat the preacher's words as beyond examination.
Neither should we.
But now we must confront the other side of this question.
Because it would be just as wrong to use the reality of spiritual abuse as an excuse to dismiss biblical generosity altogether.
The answer to manipulative giving is not a hardened heart.
The answer is redeemed giving.
Jesus said in Matthew 6:21:
"For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also."
Our relationship with money reveals something about our loves, priorities, fears, and trust.
Some believers genuinely struggle with greed.
Some possess the means to help others but refuse because they have made comfort their highest priority.
Some benefit from faithful ministry while never considering how to support its legitimate needs.
Scripture challenges those attitudes.
First Timothy 6:17–19 instructs the wealthy not to place their hope in uncertain riches, but to be generous and ready to share.
Galatians 6:6 teaches that those instructed in the word should share good things with those who teach.
First Corinthians 9:14 affirms that those who proclaim the gospel may receive their living from the gospel.
And 1 Timothy 5:17–18 recognizes appropriate support for elders who labor faithfully in preaching and teaching.
Supporting sound ministry is biblical.
Helping churches care for the needy is biblical.
Giving to advance the proclamation of the gospel is biblical.
But the reason matters.
We do not give to purchase God's love.
We give because His love has already reached us in Christ.
We do not give to prevent a pastor from cursing us.
We give because grace is transforming us into people who love God and our neighbors.
We do not give to earn salvation.
We give as people who have been saved by grace through faith.
And that difference changes everything.
In Acts 8, Simon attempted to obtain spiritual power through money.
Peter rebuked him severely.
The lesson is unmistakable: the gifts and authority of God are not commodities for sale.
The gospel is not a spiritual marketplace.
Forgiveness is not a product.
The Holy Spirit cannot be purchased.
In Matthew 10:8, Jesus told His disciples, "You received without paying; give without pay."
That statement does not prohibit the legitimate financial support of ministers, which other passages clearly affirm.
But it does remind us that God's grace must never be marketed as though it were available only to paying customers.
Consider also what Peter wrote to church elders.
In 1 Peter 5:2–3, he instructs them to shepherd God's flock willingly, not for shameful gain, and not domineering over those entrusted to their care, but by being examples.
The Greek expression μηδ᾽ ὡς κατακυριεύοντες (mēd' hōs katakyrieuontes) warns against domineering over others.
A shepherd is not supposed to rule through intimidation.
A shepherd is supposed to care for the flock.
A pastor who teaches generosity from Scripture is carrying out a legitimate responsibility.
A pastor who threatens the vulnerable to obtain their money is acting contrary to the pastoral example Peter commands.
And this is where every pastor, every ministry leader, and every Christian organization must examine itself.
Including ministries that ask for financial support.
Including ours.
Because the truth must apply equally to the person preaching it.
That would betray the very gospel we claim to defend.
So let me speak plainly about Gospel Warrior.

If these messages have helped you understand Scripture, strengthened your faith, challenged you to repent, or reminded you of the mercy of Jesus Christ, you are welcome to help this ministry continue and expand.
It is a voluntary act of support.
If you are already practicing faithful financial stewardship and have the means to help, we would be grateful for your partnership.
If you cannot afford it, please do not feel condemned.
Do not take money away from your children's necessities because you fear that God will be disappointed with you.
You can pray for this ministry.
You can share the truth.
You can encourage someone who is struggling.
You can help another believer understand the Scriptures.
These products are simply additional resources and expressions of support. They do not make anyone more spiritual, more forgiven, or more acceptable to God.
But please understand the difference between an invitation and a threat.
Not because you are afraid of what will happen if you refuse.
Not because your salvation depends on it.
Not because you must pay to prove that you love Jesus.
Because Christ has already taught us that genuine generosity is an expression of grace, not a response to extortion.
And this ministry must be willing to live under that same truth.
There is also something important that many people overlook.
You do not need money to help the gospel reach another person.
Sometimes one sincere act of sharing can put Scripture in front of someone who would never walk into a church.
Perhaps there is a friend who has quietly stopped attending services because of spiritual abuse.
Perhaps a family member has been living under fear because a religious leader told them that their poverty was proof of God's displeasure.
Perhaps someone you know still loves Jesus but no longer knows whom to trust.
Not to shame every pastor.
Not to stir up hatred toward the church.
Not to convince people that giving is unnecessary.
There may come another Sunday when a frightening statement is made from a pulpit, and you will need to return to the Scriptures rather than surrender to panic.
And now I want to ask you something more personal than whether you give ten percent, twenty percent, or any particular amount.
When you think about giving to God, what do you feel first?
Love?
Gratitude?
Trust?
Or fear?
Are you afraid that something terrible will happen if you cannot give?
Have you ever felt that your pastor's disappointment meant God had rejected you?
Have you ever sacrificed something essential because you believed you were buying protection from a curse?
Or perhaps you have been wounded so deeply by financial manipulation that you now struggle to trust any church at all.
And if you have a testimony of finding freedom through the truth of Scripture, consider sharing it.
Your story may help another person recognize that they are not alone.
You do not need to disclose private financial information or identify anyone publicly. A few honest words may be enough to encourage someone who is still suffering in silence.
Because the purpose of this conversation is not to create a crowd that despises pastors.
It is to help believers love truth, honor faithful shepherds, reject spiritual abuse, and return to Jesus.
There are many faithful pastors who serve sacrificially, preach with integrity, care for the poor, and refuse to exploit the people entrusted to them.
Thank God for those shepherds.
Pray for them.
Support them appropriately.
And when leaders misuse Scripture, respond with truth, wisdom, and accountability rather than hatred.
A church should be a place where the poor are loved, not financially cornered.
Where the wealthy are taught generosity, not promised a profitable return on every donation.
Where offerings are handled responsibly.
Where leaders are accountable.
And where Jesus Christ, not money, remains the center of worship.
Remember what happened when Jesus entered the temple and confronted those who had turned a place of worship into a marketplace.
In Mark 11:17, He spoke of God's house as a house of prayer for all nations and condemned its transformation into a den of robbers.
His anger was not directed at people who were too poor to give.
It was directed against corruption surrounding worship.
That should make every church leader tremble—not because they must fear the anger of their congregation, but because they are accountable to the Lord whose name they proclaim.
And perhaps it should comfort the struggling believer who has spent years trembling for the wrong reason.
You were afraid that God was angry because you could not afford to give.
But the Gospels reveal a Savior who confronted those who exploited the vulnerable.
You were afraid that your poverty made you worthless.
But James 2 warns Christians against showing favoritism to the wealthy while dishonoring the poor.
You were afraid that you had nothing acceptable to bring to God.
But Psalm 51:17 speaks of a broken and contrite heart that God will not despise.
You were afraid that your inability to give meant you could never be loved.
But Romans 5:8 says that God demonstrated His love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
He did not wait for us to become financially useful.
He came to save sinners.
And that brings us to the deepest truth in this entire discussion.
The greatest problem in our lives is not that we have failed to put enough money into an offering plate.
It is that we have sinned against a holy God and cannot save ourselves.
No donation can erase our guilt.
No religious performance can purchase forgiveness.
No pastor can sell us eternal life.
But Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, died for our sins and rose again.
Through Him, forgiveness is proclaimed.
Through Him, sinners are called to repentance and faith.
Through Him, broken lives can be restored.
Through Him, those who have been deceived can learn to walk in truth.
And through Him, even those who have misused religious authority can find mercy if they genuinely repent.
That is the gospel.
Not "Give me your money or God will destroy you."
But "Repent and believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, who gave Himself to save sinners."
The apostle Paul describes the heart of Christian generosity in 2 Corinthians 8:9:
"For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich."
In context, Paul uses Christ's self-giving grace to encourage generosity among believers.
The richness he describes must not be reduced to a promise that every Christian donor will become financially wealthy.
The riches of Christ's saving grace are greater than any bank account.
He gave Himself.
Not because we paid enough.
Not because we deserved it.
Not because we satisfied a preacher's financial target.
But because of grace.
And when grace truly captures the human heart, it changes the way we live.
We become more generous.
More compassionate.
More willing to support good works.
More attentive to the needs of others.
More faithful with whatever God has entrusted to us.
Not because we are being threatened.
But because we are being transformed.
That is the difference between fear-driven religion and Christ-centered discipleship.
One asks, "How much must I pay to keep God from hurting me?"
The other asks, "Lord Jesus, in view of Your mercy, how can I faithfully use what You have given me?"
One keeps people enslaved to anxiety.
The other teaches them to walk in obedience through love.
And perhaps, after everything you have read, you are finally ready to stop measuring God's love by the amount of money in your hand.
You can be poor and deeply loved by God.
You can be wealthy and desperately in need of repentance.
You can give generously and still need to examine your motives.
You can be unable to give financially and still honor Christ through prayer, service, honesty, compassion, and faithfulness.
The issue has never been whether money matters.
It does.
The issue is whether money has become a false measure of your worth before God.
And the cross answers that question forever.
Your worth is not established by the size of your offering.
Your access to God's mercy is not controlled by a pastor.
Jesus Christ is the only mediator between God and humanity, as 1 Timothy 2:5 declares.
So if someone stands before you and claims that God will curse you simply because you cannot afford to give an offering, do not answer with hatred.
Answer with Scripture.
Ask for the passage.
Read its context.
Seek counsel from mature, trustworthy believers.
Distinguish faithful teaching about generosity from threats designed to control you.
And remember that genuine spiritual authority serves under the Word of God; it does not stand above it.
If you have been using the fear of curses to pressure others into giving, there is a call for you too.
Repent.
Stop treating the vulnerable as sources of revenue.
Restore what you have wrongfully taken where possible.
Embrace accountability.
And return to the example of the Good Shepherd who laid down His life for the sheep.
Because this message is not only for wounded church members.
It is for all of us.
The giver.
The pastor.
The ministry leader.
The person who has money.
The person who has none.
Every one of us must come to the same cross.
Every one of us needs the same grace.
And every one of us must learn that the kingdom of God cannot be built faithfully through methods that contradict the character of Christ.
So tonight, if you are sitting alone, wondering whether God is disappointed because you had nothing to place in the offering plate, remember the woman from the beginning of this story.
The mother who came to church needing hope.
The mother who looked at the last money in her purse.
The mother who was made to believe she had to choose between feeding her children and escaping God's anger.
Now imagine her opening her Bible at home.
Her eyes fall on 2 Corinthians 9:7.
"Not reluctantly or under compulsion."
Then 2 Corinthians 8:12.
"According to what a person has, not according to what he does not have."
Then Romans 8:1.
"No condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus."
And slowly, for the first time in a long time, she begins to understand.
She does not have to purchase the mercy of God.
She does not have to fear that a pastor's financial disappointment has canceled the work of Christ.
She can care for her children, seek wisdom, give willingly when she is able, and continue trusting the Savior who knows her needs.
Perhaps she begins to cry again.
But this time, the tears are different.
Not because every problem has disappeared.
Not because someone promised her a miraculous financial return.
But because the gospel has begun to untangle the fear that religious pressure wrapped around her heart.
And perhaps that is what Jesus wants to do in your heart today.
Not make you careless about generosity.
Not make you bitter toward the church.
Not teach you to despise those who faithfully serve in ministry.
But free you to obey Him without being enslaved to human intimidation.
Save these Scriptures.
Because the gospel is too precious to be sold through fear.
The church is too important to be surrendered to exploitation.
And Jesus Christ is too glorious to be reduced to a financial transaction.
The Savior who gave His life to redeem you will never need a preacher's permission to love you.
